content: Pneumonia is a condition affecting the lungs and respiratory system, characterized by inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli, which are the microscopic air sacs responsible for oxygen exchange. This condition can arise from various causes, including bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic infections, as well as chemical or physical injury to the lungs. The typical symptoms of pneumonia include a persistent cough, chest pain, fever, and difficulty breathing. Diagnosis often involves chest X-rays and sputum analysis. Treatment depends on the underlying cause; for example, bacterial pneumonia is managed with antibiotics. Pneumonia is a widespread illness that affects individuals of all ages but is particularly dangerous for the elderly and those with chronic or terminal illnesses. Vaccines are available to prevent certain types of pneumonia. The prognosis varies based on the type of pneumonia, the timeliness and appropriateness of treatment, the presence of complications, and the patient’s overall health. Historically, pneumonia has been recognized since ancient times, with Hippocrates documenting its symptoms and complications. In 1875, Edwin Klebs was the first to identify bacteria in the lungs of pneumonia patients, a discovery later expanded upon by Carl Friedländer and Albert Fränkel, who identified Streptococcus pneumoniae as a causative agent. The introduction of the Gram stain technique facilitated the identification of additional pathogens. Advances in antibiotics, surgical techniques, and vaccination in the 20th century significantly reduced pneumonia-related morbidity and mortality. Pneumonia can be classified in several ways. Early classifications were based on the anatomical distribution of infection observed during autopsies or medical imaging. With advancements in microbiology, classification shifted to include etiologic groups (bacterial, viral, fungal), though identifying the specific causative agent can be challenging. More recently, pneumonia has been categorized based on the setting in which it was acquired, such as community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP), ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), and hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP). This classification is critical for guiding appropriate antimicrobial therapy. The pathophysiology of pneumonia involves the entry of bacteria or fungi into the lungs, typically through inhalation. Once in the alveoli, these microbes spread to adjacent alveoli and intercellular spaces, triggering an immune response. Neutrophils, a type of white blood cell, are recruited to the lungs to combat the infection, leading to the clinical manifestations of pneumonia. Pneumonia can result from a variety of causes, including infections by bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites, as well as chemical or physical lung injuries. The specific cause often depends on factors such as the patient’s age, immune status, geographic location, and comorbidities. Epidemiologically, pneumonia is a common illness worldwide and a leading cause of death across all age groups. Mortality rates generally decrease with age until late adulthood, but elderly individuals are at particularly high risk for pneumonia and its associated mortality. Pneumonia cases are more frequent during the winter months and are more common in males than females, as well as in African Americans compared to Caucasians. Hospitalized individuals are at increased risk of developing pneumonia, which is the second most common cause of nosocomial infections after urinary tract infections, accounting for 15–20% of cases. Risk factors for pneumonia include smoking, advanced age, immunosuppression, exposure to chemicals, and pre-existing lung diseases. The diagnosis of pneumonia involves distinguishing community-acquired pneumonia from healthcare-associated pneumonia, as these conditions differ in causative organisms, prognosis, diagnostic approaches, and treatment guidelines. Patients with pneumonia often present with a productive cough, fever, shaking chills, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, headaches, sweating, clammy skin, loss of appetite, fatigue, cyanosis, nausea, vomiting, mood swings, and joint or muscle pain. In elderly individuals, symptoms may be atypical, such as new or worsening confusion or unsteadiness leading to falls. Infants may exhibit sleepiness or reduced appetite. Physical examination findings may include fever, low body temperature, increased respiratory rate, low blood pressure, rapid heart rate, or low oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry or blood gas analysis. Patients with severe symptoms, such as difficulty breathing, confusion, or cyanosis, require immediate medical attention. Auscultation may reveal abnormal breath sounds, crackles (rales), or increased loudness of whispered speech (whispered pectoriloquy) in areas of lung consolidation. Vital signs are useful for assessing illness severity and have predictive value, though elderly patients may present with subtle symptoms. Laboratory findings, such as leukocytosis, can aid in diagnosing bacterial pneumonia and assessing patient status. Sputum samples should be collected for Gram staining and culture to identify the causative pathogen. Additional tests may include urine antigen testing, PCR, C-reactive protein, and procalcitonin levels. Chest X-rays are a key diagnostic tool for pneumonia, revealing areas of opacity (seen as white) that indicate consolidation. However, pneumonia may not always be visible on X-rays, particularly in its early stages or when it affects parts of the lung that are difficult to image. Chest CT scans, while not routinely performed, can be useful when X-ray findings are inconclusive. CT findings may include lobar consolidation, ground-glass opacities, pleural effusion, lymphadenopathy, and a tree-in-bud appearance. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage can be used to obtain samples for Gram staining and culture in certain cases, such as immunocompromised patients, ICU admissions, or antibiotic failure. Treatment of pneumonia involves three critical decisions: confirming the diagnosis, assessing the severity, and determining whether hospitalization is necessary. Most cases can be managed with oral antibiotics, rest, fluids, and home care. However, patients with severe symptoms, comorbidities, or advanced age may require more intensive treatment. Hospitalization is often necessary if symptoms worsen, home treatment fails, or complications arise. Prevention of infectious pneumonia includes treating underlying illnesses (e.g., AIDS), smoking cessation, and vaccination against pneumococcal bacteria and influenza.
